OBITUARY REFERENCES 
 MR. CHAIRMAN:  Hon. Members, I have to refer with profound sorrow to the passing away 
of Shri Chimanbhai Haribhai Shukla, Shri N.R. Da sari, Shri Thillai Villalan, Shri J. Chitharanjan, 
Shri Khan Ghufran Zahidi, Shri Harkishan Singh Surjeet and Shri Krishna Kumar Birla, former 
Members of this House. 
 Shri Chimanbhai Haribhai Shukla passed away on 21st April, 2008, at the age of 79 years. 
Born at Rajkot in Gujarat, in September, 1928, Shri Shukla had his education at Mahatma Gandhi 
Vidyalaya, Dharmendra College, Gujarat College, and LA Law College. An advocate by 
profession, Shri Shukla was asso ciated with various social welf are organisations. Shri Shukla 
started his legislative career with the membership of the Gujarat Legislative Assembly in 1967. He 
was also a Member of the Sixth Lo k Sabha. Shri Shukla represente d the State of Gujarat in this 
House from August, 1993 to August, 1999. 
 In the passing away of Shri  Chimanbhai Haribhai Shukla, the country has lost an able 
Parliamentarian. 
 Shri N.R. Dasari passed away on 27th April, 200 8 at the age of 81 years. Born at Digavalli in 
Krishna district of Andhra Pradesh, in August, 1926, Shri Dasari had his education at Nuzvid High 
School, Krishna District, Hindu College, Machilipatnam, AC College, Guntur, SRR College, 
Vijayawada, and Bangabasi College, Kolkata. A social worker, Shri Dasari participated in several 
agitations for distribution of land to the poor and  championed the cause of peasants and 
agricultural labourers and was jailed several time s. He served as National Vice-President of 
Bharatiya Khet Mazdoor Union in 2002 and also served as National Secretary of the CPI. Shri 
N.R. Dasari represented the State of Andhra Pr adesh in this House from March, 1998 to April, 
2004.  
 In the passing away of Shri N.R. Dasari, the country has lost a distinguished social  
worker. 
 Shri Thillai Villalan passed away on 20th May, 2008 at the age of 80 years. Born at 
Chidambaram, in April, 1928, Shri Villalan had his education at Annamalai University and  
Law College.  An advocate by profession,  Shri Villalan played a prominent  role  in  Self-Respect 

 2 
 
Movement in Tamil Nadu and was a founder-member of the DMK. Shri Villalan was also 
associated with various social welfare organi sations. He was a member of the Tamil Nadu 
Dramatic Advisory Committee, the Senate, An namalai University, the Tamil Nadu Tourism 
Development Committee and the Soldiers’-Sailors’ Rehabilitation Committee. Shri Villalan was 
the Editor of the Tamil Publication “Thambi” “Poomalai” and “Munnari” and Sub-Editor of 
“Dravida Nadu”. He also authored a number of novels, mostly in Tamil. Shri Villalan represented 
the State of Tamil Nadu, in this House, from April 1968 to April 1974. He was also Member of the 
Public Accounts Committee and Committee of Privileges of Rajya Sabha.  
 In the passing away of Shri Thillai Villalan, the country has lost an able Parliamentarian.  
 Shri J. Chitharanjan passed away on the 13th June, 2008 at the age of 80 years. 
 Born at Quilon in Kerala in October, 1927, Shri Chitharanjan had his education at Quilon and 
Alwaye. 
 A trade unionist, Shri Chitharanjan was actively involved in the welfare of workers and 
weaker sections of the society. He also partic ipated in the freedom struggle and student strikes 
of 1938, 1942, 1946 and 1948. Shri Chitharanjan was closely associated with the All India Trade 
Union Congress and served as its Vice-President from 1972 to October 1998, and rose to 
become its President in October 1998. Shri Chitharanjan also served as Secretary of the 
Communist Party of India.  
 Shri J. Chitharanjan started his legislativ e career with the membership of the Kerala 
Legislative Assembly and was member of that Asse mbly thrice. He also served as Minister of 
Health in the Government of Kerala from 1987 to 1988. Shri Chitharanjan represented the State of 
Kerala in Rajya Sabha from April 1997 to April 2003. He was Leader of the CPI Group in Rajya 
Sabha from 1998 to 2003. 
 In the passing away of Shri J. Chitharanjan, the country has lost a dedicated trade unionist 
and an able parliamentarian. 
 Shri Khan Ghufran Zahidi passed away on the 19th July, 2008 at the age of  
73 years. 
 Born at Etah in Uttar Pradesh in July, 1934, Shri Zahidi had his education at Government 
College, Gonda and Etawah, Christ Church  College, Kanpur and Agra University,  
Agra. 
 A journalist and a social worker, Shri Zahidi  was involved in adult education work, setting 
up of eye camps for the poor, slum clearance, and improvement of slum dwellers in and 
around Kanpur. He was  associated with several social welfare and educational institutions. He 
was President of the Urdu Academy, Uttar Pradesh, from 1993 to 1995; Chairman, Unani 
Medical College, Kanpur, 1975; and Founder Executive Member of the Mohammadia Hospital 
Society, Kanpur. He became a Member of the Uttar Pradesh State Planning Commission in 
1984. 

 3 
 
 Shri Zahidi was the Founder Member of Patrakar Sahayata Kosh Samiti, Uttar Pradesh, 
Press Club, Kanpur, and Small and Medium Newspa per Association, Delhi. He was the Editor, 
Printer, and Publisher of the ‘Daily Siyasat Jadid’, and ‘Dainik Hindi Siyasat’. 
 Shri Khan Ghufran Zahidi commenced his le gislative career with the membership of the 
Uttar Pradesh Legislative Assembly and served in that Assembly for three terms. He also served 
as Minister of Housing in the Government of Uttar Pradesh. Shri Zahidi represented the State of 
Uttar Pradesh in this House from November 1996 to July 1998 and again from July 1998 to July 
2004. 
 In the passing away of Shri Khan Ghufran Zahidi, the country has lost a distinguished 
journalist, a dedicated social worker, and an able parliamentarian. Shri Harkishan Singh 
Surjeet passed away on August 1, 2008 at the age of 92. Born at Ropowal village of 
Jhalandhar district of Punjab in March, 1916, Sh ri Surjit joined the national movement at a 
tender age of 14 and was imprisoned several times during the freedom struggle. He was 
associated with various organisations, including, the Naujwan Bharat Sabha of Shahid Bhagat 
Singh and Kirti Kisan Party. He worked tirelessly for communal harmony  and rehabilitation of 
people during partition. He was also one of th e organisers of Kishan Sabha in Punjab. Shri 
Surjeet also joined the Communist Party of India in 1935 and was General Secretary of the 
Communist Party of India-(Marxist), CPI (M ) from 1992 to 2005. A simple and dedicated 
person, he was committed to the welfare of the downtrodden sections of the society and the 
working class. Shri Surjeet began his legislative career with the Membership of the Punjab 
Legislative Assembly and was Member of that Assembly from 1953 to 1957 and again from 
1967 to 1969. Shri Surjeet represented the State of Punjab in the Rajya Sabha from April 1978 
to April 1984. Shri Harkishan Singh Surjeet had a few publications to his credit. Besides he 
had also published many pamphlets on various political and economic issues. He was editor 
of Loklehar. In the passing away of Shri Harkishan Singh Surjeet the country has lost a veteran 
freedom fighter, an able Parliamentarian and a Champion of the downtrodden and the working 
class. 
 Shri Krishna Kumar Birla passed away on th e 30th August, 2008 at the age of 89 years. 
Born at Pilani in Rajasthan in October 1918, Shri Birla had his education in Calcutta, Delhi and 
Punjab universities. He was also conferred D. Litt (Honoris Causa) by the Pondicherry University 
in 1997. An industrialist by profession, Shri K.  K. Birla was a multifaceted personality. His 
industrial empire spread across various fields  like sugar, fertilisers, chemicals to heavy 
engineering, textiles, shipping and media. He  was the Chairman of the Birla Institute of 
Technology and Science, Pilani, a premier educat ional institution. He was President of Indian 
Sugar Mills Association and Federation of Indian  Chambers of Commerce and Industry. He also 
served as Director of the Central  Board of State Bank of India and the Industrial Credit and 
Investment Corporation of India. He was trus tee of the Birla Education trust. He was  
the Chairman of the Hindustan Times and a number of  companies  in  the K. K. Birla group. 

 4 
 
 Shri Birla was the Sheriff of Calcutta in 1961. He established the K. K. Birla Foundation for 
awarding excellence in Indian literature, scientif ic research, Indian philosophy, art and culture 
and sports. Shri Birla also ha d a few publications to his credit. Shri Krishna Kumar Birla 
represented the State of Rajasthan for three terms in the Rajya Sabha from April 1984 to April 
2002 and actively participated in the debates of th e House. In the passing away of Shri Krishna 
Kumar Birla, the country has lost an eminent indu strialist, a distinguished parliamentarian, an 
educationist and a philanthropist. 
 Hon. Members, I also refer with profound sorr ow to the passing away of Field Marshal S. F. 
H. J. Manekshaw. Field Marshal Sam Manekshaw passed away on the 27 June, 2008 at the age 
of 94 years. Popularly known as Sam Bahadur, Field Marshal Manekshaw was born in Amritsar, 
Punjab in April 1914 and completed his schooling in Amritsar and Sherwood College, Nainital. He 
then joined the Indian Military Academy, Dehradun, in 1932, and was Commissioned into the 
Army in 1934. He was first attached to the Roya l Scouts, then to 12 Frontier Force Rifles, and 
later he joined the Gurkha Regiment.  
 Sam Manekshaw was a man of inspiring lead ership and was a great motivator. He had 
incisive grasp of the situation. He complemented  his professional genius and competence with 
wit and  humour, which made him popular, in general, and in the army, in particular. His 
dedication for his men to instil a sense of duty ea rned him the epithet ‘a soldier’s General.’ He 
carved out a niche for himself in the annals of the Indian Army.  
 The Field Marshal’s brilliant military strategy, decision-making, coordinating skills and, 
above all, his fine leadership was at its glorious best during the 1971 war, a moment of India’s 
crowing military achievements. 
 For his bravery, efficiency and selfless se rvice to the nation, several awards were 
conferred on Sam Manekshaw. He was decora ted with Military Cr oss during the Second 
World War and was awarded Padma Bhushan in 1968 and Padma Vibhushan in 1972. Before 
his retirement, he was made Field Marshal, th ereby becoming only the second Indian to be 
thus decorated. 
 In the passing away of Field Marshal Sam Ma nekshaw, the country has lost one of India’s 
greatest soldier and an inspiring leader.  
 We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Chimanbhai Haribhai Shukla, Shri N.R. Dasari, 
Shri Thillai Villan, Shri J. Chitharanjan, Shri Khan Ghufran Zahidi, Shri Harkishan Singh Surjeet, 
Shri Krishna Kumar Birla and Field Marshal S.H.F.J. Manekshaw. 
 I request Members to rise in their seats and observe silence for one minute as a mark of 
respect to the departed. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute)

REFERENCES BY THE CHAIR 
The victims of bomb blasts in Jaipur, Bangalore, Ahmedabad, Delhi, Modasa, 
Malegaon and Agartala and stampede at Naina Devi Temple in  
Himachal Pradesh and at Chamunda Devi Temple in Jodhpur 
 MR. CHAIRMAN:  Hon. Members, it is with utmost grief and sorrow that I refer to the 
dastardly killing of 157 innocent people in bomb blasts that took place in Jaipur, Bangalore, 
Ahmedabad, Delhi, Modasa, Malegaon and Agartala on 13th May, 25th and 26th July, 13th, 27th 
and 29th September and 1st October, 2008, respectively. More than 750 persons were reported 
to have been injured in these blasts.  
 No words are strong enough to condemn these heinous and senseless acts and I am sure 
that the whole House will join me in condemning  these acts. Such heartless acts of terrorism 
need to be dealt with firmly. On this occasion, we  express our firm resolve to fight terrorism with 
determination.  
 Hon. Members are also aware that 289 devote es, mostly women and children, were killed 
and several others injured in the twin incident s of stampede, one at Naina Devi Temple in 
Bilaspur district, Himachal Pradesh and the other at the Chamunda Devi Temple in Jodhpur, 
Rajasthan, on the 3rd August, 2008, and the 30th September, 2008, respectively. 
 The loss of so many precious lives in the bomb blasts and stampede have shocked the 
whole country. The loss suffered by the kith and kin of the deceased is irreparable. Our hearts go 
out to the bereaved families and we pray for the speedy recovery of those who were injured in 
these incidents. 
Victims of Flood in Bihar 
 MR. CHAIRMAN:  As the hon. Members are aware, arou nd the third week of August, the 
Kosi River, a tributary of the Ganges, broke through the embankments after the monsoon rains 
and wreaked death and destruction in Bihar. Lakhs of people have been displaced and 
properties worth crores have been damaged and many persons have reportedly lost their lives. 
The havoc caused by the river is unprecedented and the magnitude of loss suffered by the State 
is substantial.    
 Relief and rehabilitation measures have already been taken up on a war footing. And, efforts 
are being made to restore normalcy in the flood-affected areas of Bihar. 
 I am sure the whole House will join me in ex pressing its condolences and sympathies with

 †*1.  SHRI BRIJ BHUSHAN TIWARI: 
  SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: 
 Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
 (a)  whether it is a fact that fifteen Stat es in the country are in the grip of dengue; 
 (b)  if so, the number of persons who died of dengue and whether Government is planning 
to formulate a country-wide plan to control this disease; and 
 (c)  if so, the details thereof? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINI STER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) Dengue is generally reported from 22 States and 
Union Territories of the country. This year till 8th October, 2008, 12 States and 3 Union Territories 
have reported 3988 cases including 49 deaths. State/UT wise details are annexed as Statement. 
(See below). 
 Government of India has al ready formulated a specific disease control programme for 
Dengue for which separate budget has been allocated in 11th Five Year Plan. During 2007–08, 
Rs. 2.50 crores was sanctioned which has been  increased to Rs.16.69 crores in 2008–09. The 
following are the activities under this programme: 
 1. For strengthening monitoring and surveillance, Sentinel Surveillance Centre have been 
set up in 137 different existing hospitals sp read over 20 States and Union Territories. 
Apart from these Sentinel Surveillance Centres, 13 labs have been identified as Apex 
Referral Labs spread out in existing hospitals in different parts of the country for the 
confirmation of Dengue. 
 2. For Dengue testing, dengue testing kits (I gM MAC Elisa kits made by National Institute 
of Virology, Pune) are being supplied to the Sentinel Surveillance Hospitals and Apex 
Referral Labs. These Centres are also being fu nded to some extent by Government of 
India. 
 3. States are being funded for procurement of fogging machines. 
 4. Capacity building through training is being done. 
 5. Need based operational research is being conducted.

 6. Epidemic preparedness, Monitoring and Evaluation, and IEC for awareness generation 
of the community, are other important activities undertaken in this programme. 
 A strategic Action Plan for implementation of  above activities has been developed and sent 
to the states in January, 2007, for implementation. 
 Guidelines for Clinical Management of Dengue  have been developed and sent to the States 
for wider circulation among the hospitals. Training  has been imparted to the medical officers to 
enhance the skill in management of cases. 
 Intensified and focused IEC campaign has increased the awareness among the community 
regarding prevention of mosquito breeding in  an around their houses and early treatment 
seeking. 
 Rapid response teams were established in the affected States and districts and funds were 
provided to take prompt effective preventive measures to stop the transmission to further areas.  
 All this has resulted in better management of the cases as deaths has comparatively 
declined in 2008 and the case fatality rate has come down to 1.2% in 2008 against 1.5% in 
2006.

Infant deaths due to clinical trials at AIIMS 
 *4.  SHRI VIJAY JAWAHARLAL DARDA: 
  SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: 
 Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
 (a)  whether it is a fact that as many as  49 babies had died at the AIIMS while being 
subjected to clinical trials for testing new drugs and therapies; 
 (b)  if so, the details thereof; 
 (c)  whether Government has set up a special committee to probe reports of the deaths of 
children during clinical trials at the hospital and asked them to submit report within a week; 
 (d)  if so, the details of the report submitted by the committee; 
 (e)  whether Government proposes to re view the policy of clinical trials; and 
 (f)  if so, the details thereof? 
 T H E  M I N I S T E R  O F  S T A T E  I N  T H E  M I N I S T R Y  O F  H E A L T H  A N D  F A M I L Y  W E L F A R E  
(SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) Death of  49 children enrolled in 6 clinical trials at 
All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi, was reported between January 2006 and 
June, 2008. These consisted of 4 clinical trials with drugs as interventions, one trial with feeding 
protocol and one with Continuo us Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP). The Director, All India 
Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi, constituted a six member committee on 19th 
August, 2008, to inquire in the matter of clinical  trials under the Chairmanship of Dr. Madhuri 
Behari, Professor and Head, Department of Neurology, AIIMS, New Delhi. The Committee 
scrutinized all the clinical trials including thes e 6 studies and submitted a report which observed 
that: 
  All studies have scientific rationale and had undergone necessary scientific  
reviews. 
  All Study protocols were approved by th e Ethics Committee of AIIMS, New Delhi. 
  Permission of Drug Controller General (I) were duly obtained where required.  
  None of the deaths were attributable to the modalities tested and were due to 
underlying high risk illnesses and serious co-morbid disease conditions that the 
Children suffered from. 
  None of the mortality rates reported under these trials is higher than that reported in 
patients with similar illnesses. 
Presently, there is no proposal to review the policy of Clinical Trials.

Diseases due to untimely rains 
 * 9 .   S H R I  R A J K U M A R  D H O O T :  W i l l  t h e  M i n i s t e r  o f  H E A L T H  A N D  F A M I L Y  W E L F A R E  b e  
pleased to state: 
 (a)  whether it is a fact that untimely rain s in many parts of the country from May-June 
onward this year have given rise to diseases like malaria, gastroenteritis, etc.; 
 (b)  if so, the details thereof; and 
 (c)  the steps taken by Government to check the diseases lest they assume epidemic 
proportions? 
 T H E  M I N I S T E R  O F  S T A T E  I N  T H E  M I N I S T R Y  O F  H E A L T H  A N D  F A M I L Y  W E L F A R E  
(SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) As per the reports received from the States, 
overall there was a decline in the Malaria cases in the country during May and June 2008 and the 
current trend also indicates overa ll decline in the Malaria cases. However, the States of Andhra 
Pradesh, Goa, Maharashtra, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Punjab, Tripura, Uttarakhand, Andaman and 
Nicobar Islands and Daman and Diu have shown increase in malaria incidence during those 
months. The state wise details in this regard given as Statement. (See below) 
 Regarding cholera, the available data from National Institute of Communicable Diseases 
(NICD) laboratory and Municipal Corporation of Delhi do not show any increase in cases of 
cholera in the year 2008 as compared to the year 2007. 
 With respect to the steps taken by the Govern ment to check the diseases lest they assume 
epidemic proportions, the States were alerted in view of unusual rains during month of May–
June for taking preventive measures in respect of Malaria and other vector borne diseases. The 
situation was also reviewed with the States by the Union Secretary of Health and Family Welfare 

 18 
 
to ensure that States are adequately equipped for Epidemic Preparedness and Response 
(EPR). The States were given logistics support as per the programme norms for facilitating 
implementation of control and preventive measur es. The central teams consisting officers from 
Directorate of National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP), Regional Offices 
of Health and Family Welfare and ICMR Institutions were deputed in the identified districts to 
review the situation and to provide technical assistance. 
 NICD issues technical guidelines from ti me to time for prevention and control of 
communicable diseases including Malaria and Gast roenteritis and other waterborne diseases. In 
addition to this, NICD also carries out outbreak investigations. 
 Under the project viz. Integrated Disease Surveillance Project (IDSP) under NICO, 
information is collected on epidem ic prone diseases on weekly basis in order to generate Early 
Warning Signals of disease outbreaks and to init iate response thereto. Rapid Response Teams 
at State and district level have been constitu ted to investigate and contain the outbreaks. 
Guidelines to contain outbreaks have been prepar ed (CD Alert) and circulated to all concerned. 
Training is being imparted to Medical Officers, Para Medical Workers and Laboratory Personnels 
on outbreak investigation and diagnosis of the outbreaks. 
 NICD has deputed experts in public health in flood affected areas of Bihar from 2nd week of 
September 2008 onwards and these teams are still co ntinuing disease surveillance activities in 
Bihar. Teams provide technical support to the St ate in surveillance of communicable diseases 
and suggest measure for the prevention and control of outbreaks including Malaria and 
Gastroenteritis etc. So far, no outbreaks have been reported in the flood affected areas of Bihar. 
Surveillance is still continuing.

Rationalising of fertilizer subsidy 
 *14. SHRI RAHUL BAJAJ: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased 
to state: 
 (a)  what measures his Ministry is taking to reduce and rationalize the fertilizer subsidy;  
and 
 (b)  what have been the negative effects of the subsidy on rational use of fertilizers in the 
country? 
 THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM VILAS PASWAN): (a) and 
(b) Fertilizers subsidy is the difference between the normated delivered cost of fertilizer at farm-
gate level and the notified selling prices of subs idized fertilizer. The fertilizer subsidy has been 
increasing over the last few years due to sharp in ternational prices of raw materials/feed stock. 
Government has been encouraging investments in fertilizer sector in resource rich countries 
abroad in order to insulate the future supplies of  raw materials/feedstocks from the volatilities of 
international market. Further, a number of step s have been taken in both urea and phosphatic 
sector to improve the efficiency of the in digenous production within the country and 
consequently lead to reduction in subsidy. 
 Under New Pricing Scheme (NPS) Stage-III, fo r urea manufacturing units in the country, all 
the non-gas based units have been mandated to convert to gas by March, 2010. The energy 
norms for the production of urea has been ti ghtened as compared to NPS Stage-II. The 
production of urea above 100% of the reassess ed capacity has been encouraged through an 
incentivisation policy. Further, a policy for attrac ting new investments in Urea Sector has also 
been notified recently with an aim to encourage indigenous production of urea below import 
parity price and consequently savings in subsidy outgo. 
 In phosphatic sector, the concession scheme  with effect from 1st April, 2008, has been 
notified based on the latest recommendations of  the Tariff Commission updating the conversion 
cost of phosphatic fertilizers and consequently reducing fertilizer subsidy. 
 As regards rational use of fertilizers, a Grou p of Ministers (GoM) was constituted to look 
into the sustainable use of fertilizers and pertinent subsidy and pricing issues. The GoM has 
given a set of recommendations to promote rational  application of fertilizers in order to increase 
agricultural productivity. In pursuance of Go M recommendations, number of policy decisions 
Inter-alia including policy for production and availability of coated/fortified fertilizer in the country; 
inclusion of sulphur under the subsidy regime; ra tionalization of selling prices of subsidized 
fertilizers has been  taken by the Government over  the last one year to promote rational use of 
fertilizers.

Green revolution 
 *17.  SHRI PRABHAT JHA: Will the Minist er of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
 (a)  whether it is a fact that the first gr een revolution in the present context is not  
effective; 
 (b)  if so, whether Government has taken any steps to start second green revolution; 
 (c)  if so, the details thereof; 
 (d)  whether it is also a fact that Governme nt has identified certain  areas/ States for the 
second green revolution; and 
 (e)  if so, the details thereof with the funds allocated for the scheme? 
 THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to (e) The Green 
Revolution experienced in India paid rich divi dends and the country be came self-sufficient in 
foodgrains. However, during the past decade, th e agricultural growth rate showed a declining 
trend with production and produc tivity remaining almost stagnant . To deal with this situation, 
improvement of agricultural production and prod uctivity and enhancement of the income of the 
farmers are some of the major thrust areas id entified by the Government for focused and 
concerted action. In order to achieve these ob jectives, the National Policy for Farmers 2007, 
incorporating the key recommendations of the National Commission on Farmers, has been 
approved by the Government. In addition, a number of programmes/schemes are already under 
implementation. “Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana ”, which aims to achieve 4% annual growth in 
agriculture sector during the Eleventh Plan period by ensuring a holistic development of 
agriculture and allied sectors with an objective, Inter-alia, to incentivise States to increase public 
investment in agriculture and allied sectors has b een launched and is under implementation with 
an outlay of Rs.25,000 cr ore for the Eleventh Plan Period. Further, the “National Food Security 
Mission” is also being implemented to enhance the production of rice, wheat and pulses, with an 
outlay of Rs.4882.48 crore for the Eleventh Plan. It is targeted that the foodgrain production shall 
be increased by 20 million tonnes including National horticulture Mission, Micro Irrigation and 
National Bamboo Mission have also been launc hed by the Government. A comprehensive credit 
package was also announced by the Government in June 2004 which, Inter-alia, aimed to 
enhance flow of credit to agriculture sector and debt restructuring of outstanding loans for 
farmers in distress and in arrears. Further, the scheme of debt waiver and debt relief has been 
announced in the Union Budget for 2008–09 in order to address the problems faced by the 
farmers due to indebtedness and to enable them to access fresh institutional credit. For the year 
2008-09, the Plan outlay for Agriculture and Allied Sectors including Agricultural Research is 
Rs.12865 crore which is higher by about 60% compared to that for 2007–08.  All these schemes 
and programmes are expected to substantially increase the growth rate of agriculture sector and 
improve the income levels of the farmers.

Wastage of agricultural food items 
 *20. SHRI M.V. MYSURA REDDY: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to  
state: 
 (a)  whether it is a fact that as per Rabo India Finance Ltd. wastage of agricultural food 
items last year was to the extent of Rs. 58,000 crores; 

 31 
 
 (b)  if so, whether the wastage of agricultural food items has been on the rise over the last 
few years; 
 (c)  the extent of such wastages in the last five years, year-wise and State-wise; 
 (d)  whether his Ministry is planning to  amend the Agricultural Produce Marketing 
(Development and Regulation) Act to bring down such wastages; 
 (e)  if so, the details thereof; 
 (f)  whether any emphasis has been laid in the Eleventh Five Year Plan to address this 
serious issue; and 
 (g)  if so, the details thereof? 
 THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) As per the report of 
Rabo India Ltd., the level of wastage of agricu ltural food items is estimated to be about 
Rs.58,000 crores occurring at various stages of handling after harvesting due to fragmented 
farming, lack of  adequate post-harvest infrastr ucture such as lack of cold chain facilities, 
transportation, proper storage facilities etc. The loss due to wastages could be reduced by 
promoting the development of food processing  industries, strengthening of post harvest 
infrastructure and filling the gaps in the supply chai n. However, the substantial rate of growth of 
the food processing industry from 7% in 2003-04 to 13-14% in 2006-07 and the increase in total 
investment in food processing sector to Rs.40,000 crore in 2006-07, has contributed to 
reduction of wastages and better value addition. 
 (b) and (c) No data is being maintained about State-wise/year-wise wastage of food 
items. 
 (d) and (e) Government of India has, with a view, Inter-alia, to facilitate improving the 
supply chains to reduce wastage of agricultur al food items and improving farmers’ share in 
consumer spending, formulated a Model Agricu ltural Produce Marketing (Development and 
Regulation) Act (APMC Act) and circulated to all the States/UTs in 2003 for making necessary 
amendments in their respective APMC Acts for bringing efficiency in the existing marketing 
systems and allowing the privat e markets and development of alternative marketing channels, 
such as, direct marketing, contract farming, e-trading etc. The details of the status of 
amendment of APMC Act are give n in the enclosed Statement ( See below). To facilitate the

MSP for paddy 
 18. SHRI MOINUL HASSAN: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to  
state: 
 (a) the basis on which Government has announced Rs. 850 per quintal as Minimum 
Support Price (MSP) for paddy; 
 (b) whether Government is aware that there is a steep hike in prices of various inputs like 
fertilizers, diesel, seeds etc. in recent months which is going to be raised further; 
 (c) whether Government is also awar e that Dr. Swaminathan Commission has 
recommended for fixation of MSP on “average cost of inputs plus 50 per cent extra”; and 
 (d) if so, by when Government is going to raise MSP for paddy to Rs. 1000/- per  
quintal; 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTILAL 
BHURIA): (a) and (b) The Government decides on the Minimum Support Price (MSP) for 
various agricultural commodities taking into account the recommendations of the Commission 
for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP), the views of State Governments and Central 
Ministries as well as such other relevant factors which are considered important for fixation of 
support prices. The CACP, while formulating it s recommendations on price policy considers a 
number of important factors which includes co st of production, chan ges in input prices, 
input/output price parity, trends in market pr ices, demand and supply situation, inter-crop 
price parity, effect on industrial cost structure, ef fect on general price level, effect on cost of 
living, international market price situation and pa rity between prices paid and prices received 
by the farmers. 
 The cost of cultivation/production taken into account includes all paid out costs, such as, 
those incurred on account of hired human labo ur, bullock labour/machine labour (both hired 
and owned) and rent paid for leased in land besides cash and kind expenses on use of 
material inputs like seeds, fertilizers, manures, irrigation charges including cost of 
diesel/electricity for operation of pump sets, etc. Besides, cost of production includes 
imputed value of wages of fam ily labour and rent for owned land. The cost also covers 
depreciation of farm machinery and buildings. As such, the cost of production covers not only 
actual expenses in cash and kind but also impu ted value of owned asse ts including land and 
family labour. 

 56 
 
 During April-August, 2008 prices (in terms of Wholesale Prices Index)  of inputs such as 
fertilizers, pesticides, diesel have recorded an increase of 5.15%, 3.80% and 9.81% 
respectively. 
 (c) National Commission on Farmers (Swami nathan Commission) had recommended that 
Minimum Support Prices (MSPs) should be at least 50 per cent more than the weighted average 
cost of production. This recommendation has not been accepted by the Government since MSP 
is recommended by the Commission for Agri cultural Costs and Prices (CACP) who, Inter-alia 
takes into account various factors, like cost of prod uction of respective crops before arriving at 
their recommendations. 
 (d) The Government has already announced MSP of Rs. 850 per quintal for Paddy 
Common and Rs. 880 per quintal for Paddy Grade ‘A’ for 2008-09 season and there is no 
proposal, at present, to revise the same. Howe v e r ,  a  p r o p o s a l  t o  g r a n t  b o n u s  o f  R s . 5 0  p e r  
quintal has been approved, over and above the MSP.

Poor harvesting and mismanagement 
 26. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to  
state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that one third of India’s total crops go waste because of poor 
harvesting/mismanagement by concerned officers; 
 (b) if so, the actual figures about post harves t losses during the last three years, indicating 
whether any authoritative estimates of such lo sses are available with concerned Government 
Department; and 
 (c) if not, whether his Ministry proposes to call a meeting of State Agriculture Ministers to 
keep strict watch on such losses/mismanagement including stern anti-hording measures to 
keep check on day-by-day rise in prices? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINI STRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTILAL 
BHURIA): (a) No such information is available in the Department of Agriculture and Cooperation 
on wastage due to mismanagemen t by concerned officers. However, the post-harvest losses 
including storage losses are estimated to by around  7% in foodgrains, 30 per cent in fruits and 
vegetables and 10% of variable spices due to lack of proper post-harvest infrastructural facilities 
as per the millennium study conducted by the Ministry of Agriculture. 
 No specific study regarding wastage of foodstuff has been conducted by Department of 
Agriculture and Cooperation. However, a High Level Expert Committee on Cold Storage and 
Storage constituted by the Department of Agriculture and Cooperation, in the year 1999, had 
estimated that 25 to 30% of fruits and vegetabl es and 8 to 10% of foodgrains are lost annually 
due to lack of post-harvest t echnology and non-existence of integrated transport, storage and 
marketing facilities etc. 
 (b) Question does not arise. 
 (c) The Department of Agriculture and Cooper ation is always in touch with the State/ 
Union Territory Government for bringing out different reforms in agriculture  including  agricultural 

 65 
 
marketing for minimizing the losses and controlling anti hoarding measures through 
implementation of control orders promulgated by States under Section 3 of the Essential 
Commodities Act in certain essential commodities. 
 In order to protect the losses of foodgrains and fruits and vegetables at different stages of 
marketing, the Government of India has initiate d action on agricultural marketing reforms by 
bringing amendments in the APMC Act on the lines of Model Act circulated to all States during 
2003. The emphasis has been given to reduce the marketing channel by bringing direct 
marketing, contract farming and to improve the marketing infrastructure by involving private 
sector in development of infrastructure and setting up of markets with modern physical 
infrastructural facilities. The Ministry has also implemented capital invest ment subsidy scheme  
of Development/Strengthening of Agricultur al Marketing Infrastructure, Grading and 
Standardization, Rural Godown Scheme respectively for development of marketing infrastructure 
providing, storage facilities for farmers and othe r market participants re spectively. The market 
information is important for taki ng appropriate marketing decision s by the farmers. The Ministry 
has also launched a Central Sector Scheme of  Marketing Research and Information Network 
(AGMARKNET) since March, 2000 for disseminatio n of market information to farmers. The 
above measures initiated by the Govt. of India w ill facilitate reduction in post harvest losses of 
agricultural produce. 
National Live-stock Policy 
 27. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether it is proposed to boost the capacit y in the live-stock sector to increase growth 
in agriculture; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof; and 
 (c) the salient features of the National Live-stock Policy Inter-alia indicating the time-frame 
within which it is proposed to be implemented? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINIST RY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI TASLIMUDDIN): 
(a) to (c) Yes, Sir. 
 The salient features of the proposed National Livestock policy are as under: 
 (i) Enhancing productivity in livestock and removal of constraints which hinder 
productivity; 
 (ii) To double the availability of animal protein from the pres ent level of 10 gm. per capita 
per day to 20 gm per capita per day within a decade. 
 (iii) To improve understanding of socio eco nomic problems relating to small holding 
systems and development of appropriate extension modules for transfer of 
technology for small farm production. 
 (vi) Formulation of breeding policy for each livestock species aiming at qualitative and 
quantitative improvement in livestock products.  
 (v) To provide quality assurance in the entire  food chain to meet international standards 
concerning quality, hygiene and food safety. 

 66 
 
 (vi) Preparation of contingency plan concer ning natural calamities and disease outbreaks 
which would also include appropriate insurance packages. 
 (vii) Strengthening of educational infrastructu re for training and retraining of veterinary 
graduates, auxiliary staff as well as farmers. 
 (viii) Eradication and control of major animal diseases to improve productivity of animals 
and exploit export potential of livestock and livestock products. 
 The draft National Livestock Policy is under circ ulation before its presentation to the Cabinet 
and expected to be launched before the end of this year. 
 The National Livestock Policy provides broa d guidelines for holistic development of the 
entire livestock sector. Therefore, to meet its objectives various short, medium and long tern 
programmes will have to be implemented over a period of time. 
 Since Livestock sector is a state subject, the states will have to adopt the policy and launch 
suitable programmes specific to their needs so as  to meet the overall national objectives of 
livestock development in order to ensure food secu rity of the nation and general welfare of rural 
and urban population.

 38. SHRI TAPAN KUMAR SEN: 
  SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE: 
 Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether Tariff Commission’s recommendat ions on the issue of subsidy for complex 
fertilizers have been received by Department of Fertilizers in December, 2007; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof and its effe ct on the viability of Madras Fertilizers; 
 (c) whether it is a fact that a financial re structuring proposal of the company is pending 
before the Government since long; and 
 (d) if so, by when this will be finalized and taken up for implementation? 

 76 
 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINI STRY OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS  
(SHRI B.K. HANDIQUE): (a) Yes Sir. 
 (b) M/s Madras Fertilizers Lt d. (MFL) manufactures NPK complex fertilizer grade,  
17-17-17, MFL uses naphtha and urea mix as feedstock for manufacture of 17-17-17. The 
Tariff Commission recommended normative delivered cost of complex fertilizers group-wise 
based on the feed stock used for deriving nitrogen ‘N’, namely na tural gas, naphtha, 
ammonia-urea mix and ammonia. MFL has been grouped by the Tariff Commission in the 
naphtha group. Since there was variation in the cost of ‘N’ of different units within group, 
Individual ‘N’ price for each unit has been ad opted instead of weight ed average group price 
recommended by the Tariff Commission. For example, the weighted average group price of 
‘N’ for naphtha group in which MFL falls is Rs. 295 per ‘N’ while MFL’s cost is Rs. 326 per ‘N’. 
Adopting group average price of Rs. 295 per ‘N’ would have resulted in under recovery by 
MFL of Rs. 31 per ‘N’. As such, Government has adopted the actual cost incurred by MFL and 
thereby compensates MFL for its cost. Escalation/de-escalation in price of inputs is given 
uniformly to all units. 
 (c) and (d) A proposal for financial restructur ing of MFL is under the active consideration of 
the Government. This will also entail some commi tment/relief from Financial Institutions. Since 
the proposal also involves restructuring of the share capital of the company, the matter is under 
consultation with the minority shareholders, namely, M/s Naftiran Intertrade Company (NICO) of 
Iran whose response in the matter  is under examination. As such, it is not possible to indicate a 
firm schedule for implementation of the restructuring proposal.

 56. KUMAR DEEPAK DAS: Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether Government has any definite proposal to give relief from the price hike on 
various essential commodities including vegetable to the BPL/APL card holders; 
 (b) whether quantum of wheat, rice, sugar, kerosene etc. fixed per person per BPL/APL 
card increased sufficiently in the context of the present price hike; 
 (c) if so, the details of the response of his Ministry on price hike; and 
 (d) if not, the reason therefor? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND 
PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI TASLIMUDDIN): (a) to (c) Government has taken several 
policy decisions in order to give relief from the price hike on rice, wheat, sugar, edible oil and 
kerosene to the BPL/APL card holders as listed below. Vegetables are not distributed under 
PDS. 
1. Rice and Wheat: Allocation of foodgrains under th e Targeted Public Distribution 
System (TPDS) is made for BPL and AAY families on the basis of 1993-94 poverty 
estimates of the Planning  Commission  proj ected on the  population  estimates  of 

 103 
 
  Registrar General of India as on 1.3.2000 or  the number of families actually identified 
and ration cards issued by State Government, whichever is less. 
 Accordingly, allocations of  foodgrains (wheat, rice) fo r AAY and BPL categories are 
made @35 kg. per family per month to all accepted number of 6.52 crores families in 
the country. 
 However, allocations for APL category are made depending upon the availability of 
stocks of foodgrains in the Central Pool. Besides the normal monthly allocation for APL 
category, adhoc additional/festival allocation s of 11.45 lakh tonnes of wheat and 1.54 
lakh tonnes of rice have also been made to various States/UTs for the period July to 
December, 2008. 
2. Sugar: In order to ensure better targeting in PDS, w.e.f. 1.2.2001, the Central 
Government restricted the supply of levy sugar under PDS to BPL families except in the 
North Eastern States, Hilly States and Island  Territories where universal coverage was 
allowed to continue. Further, the Government increased the minimum per capita per 
month quantum of levy sugar distribution fr om 425 gms. to 500 gms. to benefit the 
BPL families and the population covered for supply of levy sugar under PDS was on the 
basis of the projected population as on 1st March, 2000. Accordingly, the allotment of 
levy sugar is made on the basis of fixed St ates/UTs quotas with effect from 1.2.2001. 
Besides, a quantity of about 1.00 lakh MT is  allotted as fixed Annual Festival quota of 
the States/UTs as per the scheduled festival requirement of the State Governments/UT 
Administrations. 
3. Edible Oils: The Government has launched a scheme on 28.07.2008 to distribute one  
million tons of edible oils to States/UTs at  a subsidy @ Rs.15/kg. So far, orders have 
been placed for import of 3.12 lakh tons of ed ible oils. Of this, about 2.28 lakh tone of 
edible oil has been shipped. Till 13.10.2008, 2.39 lakh tons of edible oils has landed at 
various ports in India. As on 13.10.2008, 1.43 lakh tons of edible oil has been delivered 
to various States/UTs for distribution to ration card holders @ 1 kg per ration card per 
month. 
4. Kerosene: In order to check the black marketing of Public Distribution System (PDS) 
kerosene, the Central Government have made provision in the Kerosene (Restriction 
on Use and Fixation of Ceiling Price) Order, 1993, issued under the Essential 
Commodities Act, 1955, according to which th e dealers cannot sell PDS kerosene at a 
price higher than the price fixed by th e Government or OMCs and that the PDS 
kerosene dealers should prominently displa y stock-cum-price board at the place of 
business including the place of store at a conspicuous place. With the objective of 
ensuring that the benefit of the subsidy reaches the targeted consumers in an efficient 

 104 
 
  and cost-effective manner and to preven t any leakages, Ministry of Petroleum has 
proposed introduction of Smart Card Syst em for distribution of PDS kerosene. The 
scheme is proposed to be introduced initially on an experimental basis. In the Pilot 
project, subsidized kerosene through Smart Card is proposed to be available to BPL 
families while all other ration card holders would be given non-subsidized kerosene.

Strengthening role and efficiency of PDS 
 57. SHRI N.K. SINGH: Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether Government is considering a prop osal to strengthen role and efficiency of 
Public Distribution System (PDS); and 
 (b) whether Government is also considering an y proposal to universalize access to Public 
Distribution System? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINIST RY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND 
PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) TPDS is operated under the joint 
responsibility of the Government of India and St ate/UT Governments. The Government of India 
carries out procurement of foodgr ains for the TPDS, their storage,  transportation and allocation 
to the State/UT Governments. The responsibilities for allocation foodgrains within a State/UT, 
identification of eligible BPL and AAY families based on estimates of Planning Commission and 
issuance of ration cards to them, and supervisio n of distribution of allocated foodgrains to 
eligible ration card holders through the fair price shops rest with the respective State/UT 
Governments. 
 Government has been continuously taking steps to strengthen the TPDS by improving its 
efficiency. Government got evaluated the TPDS by PEO (Planning Commission) and ORG 
MARG.. Certain shortcomings were pointed out in  their evaluation reports received in 2005. In 
view of these reports, to strengthen the TPDS an d to curb leakages and diversion of foodgrains 
meant for TPDS, in consultation with State an d UT Governments, the Government evolved a 9-
point Action Plan in 2006. This  includes meas ures such as review of  BPL and AAY lists for 
exclusion of ineligible families and inclusion of eligible families, ensuring leakage free distribution 
by taking penal action against those found indulgi ng in malpractices, involvement of Panchayati 
Raj Institutions in functioning of FPS, display of BPL and AAY lists at fair price shops, door step 
delivery of PDS commodities to fair price shops, et c. The Action Plan is under implementation in 
States and UTs since July, 2006 and is being closely monitored by FPS level Vigilance 
Committees. 
 The Government has taken various other meas ures to improve functioning of the TPDS. A 
Revised Citizen’s Charter has been issued and is being implemented since July, 2007. Monthly 
certification of delivery of allocated foodgrains to FPS and their distribution to ration card holders 

 105 
 
has been introduced from April, 2008. Training programmes for TPDS functionaries and 
awareness campaign for TPDS beneficiaries ar e being taken up. Computerization of TPDS 
operations has been initiated. Use of new techno logies such as Global Positioning System to 
monitor movement of foodgrains under TPDS has been undertaken on a pilot basis. Policy 
guidelines have also been issued on distribution of wheat flour under the TPDS, so that the poor 
families are benefited. For increasing awarenes s on TPDS, publicity-cum-awareness campaign 
is also being taken up. 
 (b) There is no such proposal un der consideration of the Government.

bailable and authorizing any gazetted office r to file prosecution for drug related 
offences.

sources follows a scientific sampling technique which avoids duplication.

across the country in different population groups. NACO has revised the operational 
guidelines for conducting HIV Sentinel Surveillance following an international consultation in 
April 2008 with the support of WHO. The next round  of HIV Sentinel Surveillance is going to be 
conducted from 1st November 2008 to 28th Febr uary 2009. HIV Sentinel Surveillance is being

Standards of Carbonated Water prescribed under Prevention of Food Adulteration (PFA) Rules,

 The National Rural Health Mission (N RHM)(2005-2012), and under its umbrella, the 
Reproductive and Child Health Programme Phase II,  launched by the Government of India in the 
year 2005, aims to improve access for rural pe ople, especially poor women and children to 
equitable, affordable, accountable and effective pr imary health care, with a special focus on 18 
States which have weak public health indicators and weak infrastructure. Under the Mission, the 
following key strategies and interventions are being implemented to accelerate the pace of 
reduction in child and maternal mortality name ly Integrated Management of Neonatal and 
Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI); New Born and Child  Care, both facility based as well as home 
based; Infant and Young Child Nutrition; Micronutrient supplementation with Vitamin A, Iron Folic 
Acid; Universal Immunization Programme (UIP); Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY), a cash benefit 
scheme to promote Institutional Delivery with a special focus on Below Poverty Line (BPL) and 
SC/ST pregnant women; Operationalising Communi ty Health Centers as First Referral Units 
(FRUs) and Primary Health Centers for 24X7 se rvices; Augmenting the availability of skilled 
manpower by means of different skill-based traini ngs such as Skilled Birth Attendance; training 
of MBBS Doctors in Life Saving Anesthetic Skills and Emergency Obstetric Care including 
Caesarian Section; Provision of Ante-natal and Post Natal Care services; prevention and 
treatment of Anemia by supplementation with Iron and Folic Acid tablets during pregnancy and 
lactation; Organizing Village Health and Nutritio n Day at Anganwadi Centers; Appointment of an 
Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) to fac ilitate accessing of health care services by the 
community including pregnant women; strengthen ing of Health Facilities, that is, District 
Hospitals, Community Health Centres (CHCs) Primary Health Centres (PHCs) and Sub Centres 
(SCs), by providing them with funds including untied grants, Annual Maintenance Grants 
(AMG) and Corpus Funds to improve service delivery.

 T H E  M I N I S T E R  O F  S T A T E  I N  T H E  M I N I S T R Y  O F  H E A L T H  A N D  F A M I L Y  W E L F A R E

August 2008 more than 6,000 severely malnourished children have been treated in Nutritional 
Rehabilitation Centers. In addition, the village h ealth nutrition days are being organized in all

provided. Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM) and Aanganwadi workers have been trained to identify

in identified 15 districts. State is also promot ing exclusive breast feeding practices along with 
initiation of breast feeding within one hour of delivery.

up, in some states like Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh, Nutrition Rehabilitation Centers at health 
facilities to manage malnourished children. Co unseling services for malnourished children are

 78. SHRI AMIR ALAM KHAN: Will the Mini ster of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be 
pleased to state: 
 (a) whether Government has carried out a su rvey on the existing health facilities and 
availability of hospital infrastructure for the rural people of the country;

medical facilities in the rural areas of the country; and

 T H E  M I N I S T E R  O F  S T A T E  I N  T H E  M I N I S T R Y  O F  H E A L T H  A N D  F A M I L Y  W E L F A R E  
(SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Yes Sir. 
 (b) The Government of India undertakes pe riodic nationwide surveys for assessing the 
impact of the health care interventions and progra mmes. In addition the latest Facility Survey in 
the country has been conducted by the Govern ment in 2003, which assessed the existing 
situation of the health care facilities available in the government health care establishments at 
different levels in India in terms of infrastructure, staff, supply and equipment at district level. The 
Facility Surveys covered various parameters of the h ealth  facilities at the District Hospital, First

equipments and drugs etc. The key results of the Facility Surv ey are given Statements I to III

Primary Health care system and provide medical facilities to citizens in rural areas. The 
National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) is the ma in vehicle for these reforms. NRHM is a flag 
ship programme of the Government launched in  2005. It has been operationalized throughout 
the country, with special focus on 18 states which includes 8 Empowered Action Group States 
(Bihar, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisga rh, Uttar Pradesh, Utta ranchal, Orissa and 
Rajasthan), 8 North-East States, Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir. The National 
Rural Health Mission seeks to provide accessible, affordable and quality health care to the 
rural population, especially to the poor and the vulnerable sections of the population. It also 
seeks to reduce Maternal Mortality Ratio, Infa nt Mortality Rate and the Total Fertility level 
within the seven year period of the Mission,  ending in 2012. The Mission seeks to provide 
accountable, effective, reliable, and quality primary health care through creation of a cadre of 
Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHA), strengthening of Public Health Delivery System at 
all levels, improved hospital care measured through Indian Pubic Health Standards (IPHS), 
provision of untied funds to all the facilitie s to enable local action, decentralization of 
Programme to district level to improve intra and inter-sectoral convergence and effective 
utilization of resources. Flexibility has been given to the States to devise need based 
Programme Implementation Plan. 
 (d) The Eleventh Plan approved outlay provides for Rs. 41,092.92 crores for Health; Rs. 
90,558 crores for NRHM and Rs. 4,496.08 crores for Health Research.

in Goa and the situation of malaria is monitored continuously and the State Government is also 
taking control measures, which include intensive surveillance, screening of migratory labourers, 
complete treatment of malaria positive cases, in tensive larviciding in and around construction 
sites and mobilization of community as well as builders for taking up control measures. The State 
has also introduced bye-laws under which all labour population are screened for malaria on their 
arrival and provided treatment.

 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINIST R Y  O F   H E A L T H  A N D  F A M I L Y  W E L F A R E  
(SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) Death of  49 children enrolled in 6 clinical trials 
at All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi was reported between January 2006 and 
June, 2008. These consisted of 4 clinical trials with drugs as interventions, one trial with feeding 
protocol and one with Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP). It was observed that 4142 
children were enrolled in 42 clinical trials in the Department of Paediatrics. 
 (c) and (d) Yes, Sir. In one case, the fore ign manufactured medicines were used during 
the trials. Zinc deficiency is of public health  importance in India because of the problem of 
widespread zinc deficiency. WHO/UNICEF, Indian Academy of Pediatrics and the National Rural 
Health Mission, Govt. of India recommend use of zinc in treatment of acute diarrhea in all infants 
and children. This policy is based on large well  done randomized controlled studies from many 

 147 
 
developing countries, and different parts of India including AIIMS. Zinc is important in human 
biology and its deficiency impairs various immune and non immune defence against infections. 
Low levels of zinc in the cord blood and in infants, particularly so in the low birth weight, who 
constitute one-third of all births in India and co ntribute maximally to the increased infant deaths. 
Neonatal sepsis is an important cause of death in  these infants. The intent of the study was to 
provide a cheap, safe and efficacious treatment in  addition to antibiotics for serious bacterial 
infection in neonates and young infants. The Government of India has been encouraging the 
public sector companies and the drug industry to prepare cheap dispersible zinc tablets. The 
Lancet has rated use of zinc in sick children in diarrhea as one of the 10 essential interventions 
for all child health programmes in the developing world. 
 (e) 1073 children were admitted for these clinical trials and 42 clinical trials were conducted 
on these children.

written consent were obtained from the parents/guardians of the children.

both for meeting passenger and freight needs, in synchronization with the requirement of the 
growing economy, has placed considerable burden on the Railways are also not getting 
adequate gross budgetary support and are increasingly relying on internal generation and

Price hike of steel 
 153. SHRI S. ANBALAGAN: Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether the Government is aware of the co ntinuous increase in price of steel which is 
detrimental to house construction effects of the people; 
 (b) if so, the price fixing mechanism for stee l and extent to which the price of the steel 
increased during each of the last six months; and 

 186
 (c) the steps being taken by Governme nt to stabilize the price of steel? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (SHRI JITIN PRASADA): (a) Price 
of steel across all categories in the domestic as  well as the internatinoa l markets witnessed an 
uptrend since January, 2008 onwards. However, a number of fiscal and administrative measures 
timely taken by the Government, as mentioned below in reply to part (c) of the question, helped 
in stabilizing the steel prices in the domestic ma rket. The effect of rise in price of steel on 
construction is limited and varies depending upon the type, the size and the qualtiy of 
construction. 
 (b) Steel is a deregulated sector and steel pr ices are determined by the market based on 
factors like demand and supply situation, landed cost of imports, input costs and price and 
availability of substitutes etc. The details of pric e movement of representative categories of steel 
products on monthly basis during the last six months in the retails market of Delhi is given in the 
Statement. (see below) 
 (c) The steps taken by the Government to stabilize steel prices in the country are as 
follows:– 
  DEPB on steel products withdrawn w.e.f. 27.3.08. 
  Import Duty on all non-alloy steel, Zinc, ferro-alloys and metcoke revised to ‘Nil’ from 
5%, w.e.f. 29.4.08 CVED on TMT bars and rounds modified to ‘Nil’ from 14%. 
  Export Duty @ 15% imposed on 10.5.08 in Pig Iron, Sponge, Iron, Scrap, Ingots and 
all categories of non-alloy semi finished steel still continues. 
  Export Duty @ 10% was imposed on long products such as bars, wire rods, angles 
etc., on 10.5.08. This war later revised to 15% w.e.f. 13.6.08. 
  Ad-valorem export duty of 15% imposed on iron ore of all categories and grades.

Increase in price of iron ore 
 155. SHRI DHARAM PAL SABHARWAL: Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to  
state: 

 189
 (a) whether it is a fact that Government is considering various measures to check and 
contain the prices of iron ore including ban on export of iron ore; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof; 
 (c) whether Government is aware that steel manufacturers are facing a lot of hardships 
due to increase in prices of iron ore; and 
 (d) if so, the steps being taken to  contain the prices of iron ore? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (SHRI JITIN PRASADA): (a) and 
(b) With a view to make available iron ore to domestic iron and steel industry at an affordable 
price, Government of India has imposed an ad-valorem export duty of 15% on all varieties of 
iron ore w.e.f. 13th June, 2008. However, ban on export of iron ore is presently not under 
consideration of the Government. 
 (c) and (d) It has been brought to notice by sponge iron producers and pig iron 
producers, who procure iron ore mainly on spot basis, that they are facing problems in getting 
iron ore supply at affordable prices, thereby affecting their economic viability. However, recently, 
the spot prices of iron ore in  the global market have witne ssed a declining trend. This is 
expected to result in decrease in the domestic prices of iron ore also.

DISQUALIFICATION OF A MEMBER ON GROUND OF DEFECTION 
 MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon’ble Members, I have to make the following announcement: 
 Shri Veer Singh, Member, Rajya Sabha, filed before the then Chairman, Rajya Sabha, 
Shri Bhairon Singh Shekhawat, a petition da ted 4th April 2007, under paragraph 6 of the 
Tenth Schedule to the Constitution and Rule 6 of the Members of Rajya Sabha 
(Disqualification on grounds of Defection) Rules, 1985, praying that the Chairman, Rajya 
Sabha, be pleased to hold that Shri Isam Singh, Member, Rajya Sabha, stands 
disqualified under the Tenth Schedule to the Constitution of India and also declare his 
seat in the Rajya Sabha vacant. The then Chairman forwarded copies of the petition and 
the annexures thereto to Shri lsam Singh and Sushri Mayawati, the then Leader of the 
Bahujan Samaj Party in Rajya Sabha, under rule 7(3) of the said Rules, on the 20th of 
April, 2007, requesting them to forward their comments on the petition to him within 
seven days from the receipt of the same. 
 Sushri Mayawati in her comments agreed with the contention of the petitioner and 
contended that Shri ls am Singh, who had been  elected to the Rajya Sabha from the State of 
Uttar Pradesh as a candidate of the Bahujan Samaj Party , was expelled from the party for 
violating the party norms and for anti-party activities. Further, his act of forming a new political 

 195
party “Bahujan Kranti Party ” on the 10th September, 2006 and his becoming its National 
President is a conduct that indicates that he has voluntarily given up the membership of the 
Bahujan Samaj Party and, therefore, be disqualified w.e.f. 10th September, 2006. 
 Shri Isam Singh in his comments disagreed wi th the charges made against him. Shri Isam 
Singh contested the contents of the petition. He denied having received any Show Cause Notice 
and said that it was a manipulated document meant for his harassment. In fact, he came to 
know about his suspension from the Party from media. He denied making false allegations 
against Sushri Mayawati and accused her of taking a dictatorial action, when he tried to uplift the 
image of the Party. Shri Isam Singh denied the charges of voluntarily giving up membership of 
the Bahujan Samaj Party and joining a new political party. He also stated that he had formed a 
new political party only after his expulsion from the BSP, and hence there was no question of his 
disqualification as a Member of Rajya Sabha. He requested that Shri Veer Singh’s petition 
seeking his disqualification may be dismissed. 
 After considering the comments of Sushri Mayawa ti as well as of Shri Isam Singh in relation 
to the petition, the then Chairman was satisfied, having regard to the nature and circumstances 
of the case that it was necessary to refer the petition to the Committee of Privileges of the Rajya 
Sabha for making a preliminary inquiry and submitting a report to him, under sub-rule (4) of 
Rule 7 of the Rules and ordered accordingly on 24th July, 2007. 
 The Committee of Privileges submitted it s Report to me on the 22nd May, 2008. 
 On receipt of this Report, I forwarded a copy thereof to Shri Isam Singh and gave him 
opportunities to appear before me on July I and 4, 2008 to represent his case and to be heard in 
person in terms of Rule 7 (7) of the Members of Rajya Sabha (Disqualification on ground of 
Defection) Rules, 1985. 
 Taking into account the facts of the case and the report of the Committee of Privileges and 
in accordance with the provisions of article 102 (2) read with the Tenth Schedule to the 
Constitution of India, I decided and declared by an order as follows: 
 “In exercise of the powers conferred upon me under article 102(2) read with paragraph 6 of 
the Tenth Schedule to the Constitution of India, I, Mohammad Hamid Ansari, Chairman, 
Rajya Sabha, hereby decide th at Shri lsam Singh, an elec ted member of the Rajya Sabha 
from the State of Uttar Pradesh, by voluntarily giving up his membership of the Bahujan 
Samaj Party, his original political party, has become subject to disqualification for being a 
Member of the Rajya Sabha in terms of paragraph 2(1)(a) of the Tenth Schedule to the 
Constitution of India.” Accordingly, Shri Isham Singh has ceased to be a Member of Rajya 
Sabha with effect from 4th July, 2008.
